questions.question: In the Datadog System check, what does the `system.cpu.system` metric measure?
choices: Percent of time the CPU spent running user space processes
Percent of time the CPU spent running the kernel
Percent of time the CPU spent waiting for I/O to complete
Percent of time the CPU spent in an idle state
questions.explanation: Datadog documents `system.cpu.system` as the percent of time the CPU spent running the kernel (system calls, drivers, interrupt handling). Time spent in application code is `system.cpu.user`, time stalled on storage is `system.cpu.iowait`, and time with nothing to do is `system.cpu.idle`.

questions.question: A cloud VM becomes sluggish even though its workload has not changed. Datadog shows `system.cpu.stolen` jumping to 25%. What does this indicate?
choices: Processes on the VM are waiting for disk reads and writes to finish
The kernel is busy handling system calls and hardware interrupts
The hypervisor is giving physical CPU time to other virtual CPUs
A low-priority (niced) process is consuming most CPU cycles
questions.explanation: `system.cpu.stolen` is the percent of time the virtual CPU spent waiting for the hypervisor to service another virtual CPU, and it only applies to virtual machines. High steal is the classic 'noisy neighbor' symptom, fixed by resizing or moving the VM rather than tuning the app. Waiting on disk would show up as `system.cpu.iowait`, and kernel work as `system.cpu.system`.

questions.question: A Linux host shows low `system.cpu.user` and `system.cpu.system` but consistently high `system.cpu.iowait`. Which resource is the most likely bottleneck?
choices: Storage I/O, such as a slow or saturated disk
CPU capacity, because all cores are fully busy
The hypervisor, which is taking CPU from this VM
The network interface, which is dropping packets
questions.explanation: `system.cpu.iowait` is the percent of time the CPU spent waiting for I/O operations to complete, so a high value with low user and system time points to storage that cannot keep up. Busy cores would show high user or system time, hypervisor contention appears as `system.cpu.stolen`, and network problems show up in `system.net.*` metrics rather than iowait.

questions.question: Which statement about the Linux load average reported by `system.load.1`, `system.load.5`, and `system.load.15` is correct?
choices: It is a percentage of CPU busy time that ranges from 0 to 100
It is collected by the Agent only on Windows hosts
It measures network requests queued per second on the host
It is a count of tasks, averaged over 1, 5, and 15 minutes
questions.explanation: Load average is the number of tasks that are running, runnable, or waiting for disk I/O, averaged over 1, 5, and 15 minutes. It is a count, not a percentage, so it has no fixed upper limit. Datadog marks the `system.load.*` metrics as Linux only, and they have nothing to do with network request queues.

questions.question: A Linux host reports a `system.load.1` of 12 while `system.cpu.idle` stays around 70%. What best explains a high load average with mostly idle CPUs?
choices: Load average only counts processes owned by the root user
Load average also counts tasks blocked waiting on disk I/O
Load average counts only tasks currently running on a CPU
Load average includes time stolen by the hypervisor
questions.explanation: On Linux, the load average counts tasks in the run queue (state R) and tasks in uninterruptible sleep waiting for disk I/O (state D). Many processes stuck on slow storage raise the load without using CPU, so check `system.cpu.iowait` and disk metrics next. Load is not limited to root processes or to tasks currently on a CPU, and steal time is reported separately as `system.cpu.stolen`.

questions.question: A Linux host with 4 CPUs reports `system.load.1` = 8. What would `system.load.norm.1` show, and what does it suggest?
choices: 2; about twice as many tasks want to run as there are CPUs
32; the load is multiplied by the CPU count to show total demand
0.5; the host is using roughly half of its CPU capacity
8; normalization only changes the value on single-CPU hosts
questions.explanation: `system.load.norm.1` is the one-minute load average normalized by the number of CPUs, so 8 / 4 = 2. A normalized value above 1 means more tasks are running or waiting than there are CPUs, so work is queuing. Normalizing lets a single monitor threshold work across hosts of different sizes.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of swap space on a Linux host?
choices: A reserved area of RAM that caches recently read disk blocks
A faster memory tier that sits between the CPU and main RAM
Disk space that holds memory pages when physical RAM is full
A temporary partition that stores files written to `/tmp`
questions.explanation: Swap is a dedicated partition or file on disk; when RAM is full, inactive memory pages are moved there. Because disks have a much slower access time than RAM, heavy swapping hurts performance. Caching disk blocks in RAM is the page cache (`system.mem.cached`), and the tier between the CPU and RAM is the CPU cache.

questions.question: On a Linux host, `system.swap.used` climbs steadily while application latency increases. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The filesystem has run out of inodes, so new files cannot be created
The CPU is overheating and throttling its clock speed to cool down
The network interface is dropping packets under heavy load
RAM is exhausted, so memory pages are being moved to slower disk
questions.explanation: Growing swap usage means the kernel is moving memory pages out of physical RAM into swap space on disk, which is far slower than RAM, so applications slow down. Check `system.mem.usable` and per-process memory to find the cause. Inode exhaustion causes file-creation errors, and packet drops appear in `system.net.*` metrics, not in swap.

questions.question: Which Datadog metric best shows how much RAM is actually available for new applications on Linux, because it accounts for reclaimable cache?
choices: `system.mem.free`
`system.mem.usable`
`system.mem.cached`
`system.mem.total`
questions.explanation: `system.mem.usable` uses MemAvailable from `/proc/meminfo` when present, or falls back to free + buffered + cached memory. `system.mem.free` counts only completely unused RAM, which is often low on healthy Linux hosts because the kernel uses spare memory for cache. `system.mem.cached` is only the cache portion, and `system.mem.total` is all physical RAM.

questions.question: Compared with a hard disk drive (HDD), what is a defining characteristic of a solid state drive (SSD)?
choices: It uses flash memory and has no moving parts
It stores data on spinning magnetic platters
It is usually cheaper per gigabyte of capacity
It performs well only with large sequential I/O
questions.explanation: SSDs store data in nonvolatile flash memory with no mechanical components, which makes them faster and more durable. HDDs use spinning magnetic platters and a moving read/write head, cost less per GB, and perform best with large sequential I/O, while SSDs also handle random I/O efficiently.

questions.question: A database performs a very high number of small, random reads and writes. Which storage performance characteristic matters most for this workload?
choices: Sequential throughput in MiB per second
Total raw capacity of the disk in gigabytes
IOPS (input/output operations per second)
Number of inodes available on the filesystem
questions.explanation: IOPS counts how many read and write operations a device completes per second, which is what limits workloads made of many small, random I/Os. Throughput (bytes per second) matters more for large sequential transfers such as backups or streaming. Capacity and inode counts limit how much you can store, not how fast operations complete.

questions.question: `system.disk.in_use` for `/var` shows only 40% of space used, yet applications fail with "No space left on device" when creating new files. Which metric should you check next?
choices: `system.disk.write_time_pct`
`system.mem.pct_usable`
`system.swap.pct_free`
`system.fs.inodes.in_use`
questions.explanation: Every file consumes an inode, and a filesystem holding millions of small files can run out of inodes while plenty of blocks remain; file creation then fails with "No space left on device". The Disk check reports `system.fs.inodes.in_use`, and `df -i` shows the same on the host. The other metrics measure disk busy time, memory, and swap, none of which explain this error.

questions.question: A monitor alerts when `system.disk.in_use` is above 90, but it never triggers, even when disks are nearly full. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The metric is a fraction from 0 to 1, so the threshold should be 0.9
The metric is reported in bytes, so the threshold must be a byte count
The metric is only collected on Windows hosts, not on Linux hosts
The Disk check is disabled by default and must be enabled first
questions.explanation: The Disk check reports `system.disk.in_use` as a fraction of total space (0 to 1), so a disk that is 95% full reports 0.95 and never exceeds 90. Use a threshold of 0.9, or use `system.disk.utilized`, which is expressed as a percentage. `system.disk.used` is the byte-based metric, and the Disk check is enabled by default.

questions.question: An EC2 instance has 2 physical CPU cores with simultaneous multithreading enabled (2 threads per core). How many vCPUs does its operating system see?
questions.explanation: With simultaneous multithreading (such as Intel Hyper-Threading), each core runs two hardware threads, and each thread is presented to the OS as a vCPU: 2 cores x 2 threads = 4 vCPUs, exactly like an m5.xlarge. The OS schedules work across these 4 logical CPUs; 2 would be the physical core count only.

questions.question: What does a CPU clock speed of 3.0 GHz describe?
choices: The CPU can hold 3 GB of data in its cache
The CPU has 3 physical cores available to the OS
The CPU can transfer 3 GB per second to RAM
The CPU runs about 3 billion cycles per second
questions.explanation: Clock speed is the number of cycles a CPU executes per second, expressed in gigahertz (billions of cycles per second), so 3.0 GHz means about 3 billion cycles per second. It is unrelated to cache size, core count, or memory bandwidth; overall performance depends on clock speed together with cores, threads, and architecture.

questions.question: What is a key architectural difference between a container and a virtual machine (VM)?
choices: Containers need a hypervisor; VMs run directly on the host kernel
Containers include a full guest OS; VMs only package app binaries
Containers share the host's kernel; each VM runs its own OS kernel
Containers run only on bare metal; VMs run only in public clouds
questions.explanation: A container is an isolated process that shares the host's kernel, which makes it lightweight and fast to start. A VM runs a complete operating system with its own kernel and drivers on top of a hypervisor. The other options reverse these roles, and both technologies run on-premises and in the cloud.

questions.question: What distinguishes a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor from a Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor?
choices: It runs directly on the physical hardware, not on a host OS
It runs as an application on top of a desktop operating system
It shares the host kernel with containers instead of running VMs
It can run only a single virtual machine per physical server
questions.explanation: A Type 1 hypervisor such as KVM, Hyper-V, or VMware ESXi is installed directly on the server hardware and allocates resources to VMs itself. A Type 2 hypervisor such as VirtualBox or VMware Workstation runs as an application on a host operating system, which adds overhead. Both types can run many VMs, and sharing a kernel describes containers, not hypervisors.

questions.question: According to Datadog's billing documentation, what counts as a host?
choices: Only physical servers where the Datadog Agent package is installed
Any container that sends metrics to a containerized Datadog Agent
Each unique IP address that sends data to a Datadog intake endpoint
Any physical or virtual OS instance that you monitor with Datadog
questions.explanation: Datadog defines a host as any physical or virtual OS instance that you monitor, such as a server, a VM, a Kubernetes node, an Azure App Service Plan instance, or a Heroku dyno. Physical-only is too narrow, containers monitored by a per-host Agent are not hosts themselves, and IP addresses are not the unit being counted.

questions.question: A team installs the Datadog Agent inside every application container instead of running one containerized Agent per host. How does this affect the billable host count?
choices: Only the underlying node counts, however many Agents run on it
Each container running its own Agent is counted as a host
Containers are never counted as hosts in any configuration
Each container counts as a fraction of the underlying node
questions.explanation: Datadog recommends a single containerized Agent per host, which collects both container and host metrics. If you install the Agent directly in each container, each container is counted as a host from a billing perspective. That is why the per-container approach is discouraged, and why the 'never counted' and 'fraction' options are wrong.

questions.question: An engineer runs `uname -m` on a server and sees `x86_64`. What does this tell them?
choices: The kernel release number is 86.64
The system has 64 GB of RAM installed
The machine uses a 64-bit x86 architecture
The host runs on 64-bit ARM (aarch64) hardware
questions.explanation: `uname -m` prints the machine hardware name; `x86_64` means a 64-bit x86 processor, while 64-bit Arm appears as `aarch64`. The kernel release comes from `uname -r`, and installed RAM is shown by `free`. This matters for Datadog because Agent 7 is listed for 64-bit x86 and 64-bit Arm v8 platforms.

questions.question: Why is a 64-bit operating system preferred over a 32-bit one on a server with 32 GB of RAM?
choices: 32-bit addresses can reference only about 4 GB of memory
32-bit systems cannot run more than one process at a time
64-bit systems do not need swap space or a page cache
64-bit systems double the clock speed of the same CPU
questions.explanation: A 32-bit address can represent 2^32 distinct byte addresses, about 4 GB, so a 32-bit OS cannot use large amounts of RAM efficiently, while a 64-bit OS handles large memory natively. Bit width does not change clock speed, 32-bit systems multitask normally, and 64-bit systems still use swap and page cache.

questions.question: Which Datadog metric should you graph to see inbound traffic volume on a host's network interfaces?
choices: `system.net.bytes_sent`
`system.io.block_in`
`system.net.packets_in.error`
`system.net.bytes_rcvd`
questions.explanation: `system.net.bytes_rcvd` is the number of bytes received on a device per second, reported by the Network check, which the Agent enables by default. `system.net.bytes_sent` measures outbound traffic, `system.net.packets_in.error` counts receive errors rather than volume, and `system.io.block_in` is disk I/O, not network.

questions.question: Which of these System check metrics does Datadog document as available on Linux only?
choices: `system.cpu.user`
`system.mem.pct_usable`
`system.load.norm.5`
`system.swap.free`
questions.explanation: The System check marks every `system.load.*` metric, including the CPU-normalized `system.load.norm.*` variants, as Linux only. CPU user time, memory, and swap metrics carry no Linux-only note in the metric list; CPU and memory metrics are collected on Windows hosts too.

questions.question: Which command displays the distribution name and version of a Linux host?
choices: `cat /etc/os*`
`uname -n`
`hostname`
`cat /etc/hostname`
questions.explanation: The glob `/etc/os*` matches `/etc/os-release`, which contains operating system identification data such as NAME, VERSION, ID, and PRETTY_NAME. `uname -n` prints the network node hostname, and both `hostname` and `/etc/hostname` give the host's name, not its distribution or version.

questions.question: What is the main difference between the Linux and Windows operating systems?
choices: Linux has no graphical desktop, while Windows does
Linux is open source, while Windows is proprietary
Linux is inherently more secure than Windows
Linux runs only on servers, while Windows runs on desktops
questions.explanation: Linux is an open source operating system released under the GNU GPL, so anyone can run, study, modify, and redistribute its source code; Windows is proprietary Microsoft software. Linux distributions offer graphical desktops such as GNOME and KDE, security depends on configuration rather than the OS family, and both systems run on servers and desktops.

questions.question: On a Linux host, in which directory is the Datadog Agent's main configuration file, `datadog.yaml`, located?
choices: `/opt/datadog-agent/`
`/var/log/datadog/`
`/etc/datadog-agent/`
`/home/dd-agent/`
questions.explanation: Following the Linux convention that `/etc` holds machine-local configuration, the Agent's main file is `/etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml`, and integration configs live in `/etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/`. `/opt/datadog-agent/` is the installation directory, and `/var/log/datadog/` holds the Agent's log files.

questions.question: Which pairing of a Linux directory and its purpose is correct?
choices: `/opt` - add-on application packages
`/etc` - temporary files cleared at boot
`/proc` - home directories for users
`/tmp` - machine-local configuration files
questions.explanation: The filesystem hierarchy reserves `/opt` for add-on packages, which is why the Datadog Agent installs into `/opt/datadog-agent`. `/etc` holds machine-local configuration files, `/tmp` holds temporary files that may be deleted without notice, `/home` holds user home directories, and `/proc` is the mount point of the proc filesystem.

questions.question: The Agent reads memory statistics such as MemAvailable from `/proc/meminfo`. What kind of filesystem is mounted at `/proc`?
choices: A disk partition reserved for storing program binaries
A RAM-backed folder for temporary files deleted at reboot
A network share mounted from a central configuration server
A pseudo-filesystem exposing kernel and process information
questions.explanation: `/proc` is the mount point of the proc filesystem, a pseudo-filesystem that provides information about running processes and the kernel; its files are generated by the kernel rather than stored on disk. Tools like `free`, `top`, and the Datadog Agent read files such as `/proc/meminfo` and `/proc/loadavg`. Program binaries live in `/usr/bin`, and temporary files go in `/tmp`.

questions.question: You want to watch new entries appear in `/var/log/datadog/agent.log` in real time while restarting the Agent. Which command should you use?
choices: `tail -n 10 /var/log/datadog/agent.log`
`tail -f /var/log/datadog/agent.log`
`head -n 20 /var/log/datadog/agent.log`
`cat /var/log/datadog/agent.log`
questions.explanation: `tail -f` (follow) prints the end of the file and then keeps outputting appended data as the file grows, until you press Ctrl+C. `tail -n 10` prints the last 10 lines once and exits, `head -n 20` prints the first 20 lines, and `cat` prints the whole file once.

questions.question: You need every line containing "error" in `agent.log`, regardless of case (ERROR, Error, error). Which command does this?
choices: `grep -v error agent.log`
`grep -c error agent.log`
`grep -i error agent.log`
`grep -l error agent.log`
questions.explanation: `grep -i` ignores case distinctions, so it matches ERROR, Error, and error. `-v` inverts the match and prints lines that do not contain the pattern, `-c` prints only a count of matching lines, and `-l` prints only the names of files that match.

questions.question: What does the command `ps aux | grep datadog` do?
choices: Sends the full process list to grep, which shows only lines mentioning datadog
Runs ps and grep one after the other and saves both outputs to a file named datadog
Stops every running process whose command name contains the word datadog
Starts the Datadog Agent in the background and prints its process ID
questions.explanation: The pipe `|` connects the standard output of `ps aux` (every process on the system) to the standard input of `grep`, which filters it down to lines containing "datadog". It is a quick way to check whether Agent processes are running. Pipes do not write to files (that is redirection with `>`), and neither command stops or starts processes.

questions.question: A cron job runs `echo "check ok" >> /tmp/health.log`. What happens if `/tmp/health.log` already exists?
choices: The file is overwritten and now contains only the new text
The command fails because the target file already exists
The text is printed to the terminal and the file is unchanged
The text is appended to the end of the existing file
questions.explanation: `>>` opens the file for appending, so each run adds a line to the end (and creates the file if it does not exist). A single `>` would truncate the file and overwrite its contents. Neither operator fails on an existing file, and redirection sends the output to the file instead of the terminal.

questions.question: Which signal does `kill <PID>` send when no signal is specified?
choices: `SIGTERM`, which asks the process to terminate gracefully
`SIGKILL`, which forces the process to end immediately
`SIGHUP`, which traditionally tells a daemon to reload its config
`SIGSTOP`, which pauses the process until it is resumed
questions.explanation: If no signal is specified, `kill` sends TERM (signal 15), which the process can catch to clean up before exiting. KILL (signal 9) must be requested explicitly, for example with `kill -9`. HUP and STOP are likewise only sent when you name them.

questions.question: A hung process ignores `kill 1234`. The admin then runs `kill -9 1234`, and the process exits immediately. Why did the second command work?
choices: Signal 9 gives the process nine seconds to shut down cleanly
Signal 9 (SIGKILL) cannot be caught or ignored by the process
The -9 flag repeats the default signal nine times in a row
The -9 flag makes kill run with root privileges automatically
questions.explanation: `kill -9` sends SIGKILL, which a process cannot catch, block, or ignore, unlike the default SIGTERM that a process may handle or ignore. Because the process gets no chance to clean up, SIGKILL should be a last resort. The number selects the signal; it is not a timeout or a repeat count, and it does not grant privileges.

questions.question: A disk space monitor fires for `/`. You want a quick, human-readable summary of used and available space on every mounted filesystem. Which command should you run?
choices: `du -sh`
`free -h`
`df -h`
`ls -lh`
questions.explanation: `df` displays the space available on mounted filesystems (all of them when no file is given), and `-h` prints sizes in human-readable units. `du -sh` totals the space used by files under a directory, `free -h` reports memory rather than disk, and `ls -lh` lists individual files with their sizes.

questions.question: After finding `/var` nearly full, you want a single human-readable total of how much space the `/var/log` directory tree uses. Which command gives it?
choices: `df -i /var/log`
`ls -a /var/log`
`find /var/log -type d`
`du -sh /var/log`
questions.explanation: `du` summarizes disk usage recursively; `-s` displays only a total for each argument and `-h` uses human-readable sizes. `df -i` shows inode usage for the whole filesystem, `ls -a` just lists entries including hidden ones, and `find -type d` only lists directories.

questions.question: Which command shows total, used, free, and available physical memory and swap on a Linux host?
choices: `free -h`
`df -h`
`lscpu`
`hostnamectl`
questions.explanation: `free` parses `/proc/meminfo` and displays used and free physical and swap memory, including buffers, cache, and an 'available' estimate; `-h` scales the units. `df -h` reports disk space, `lscpu` shows CPU architecture details, and `hostnamectl` shows the hostname and OS information.

questions.question: A file's permissions are set with `chmod 644 app.conf`. What access does this grant?
choices: Owner: read/write/execute; group and others: read/execute
Owner: read/write; group: read; others: read
Owner: read; group: read/write; others: read/write
Owner, group, and others: read/write
questions.explanation: Each octal digit is the sum of read (4), write (2), and execute (1), and the three digits apply to the owner, the group, and others. So 6 means read + write for the owner, and 4 means read-only for group and others (`rw-r--r--`), which is typical for config files. `755` would be `rwxr-xr-x`, and `666` would give everyone read/write.

questions.question: The Agent cannot write its logs because `/var/log/datadog/` is owned by root. Which command, from Datadog's permission troubleshooting docs, fixes the ownership?
choices: `sudo chmod -R dd-agent:dd-agent /var/log/datadog/`
`sudo chgrp -R root:dd-agent /var/log/datadog/`
`sudo su dd-agent /var/log/datadog/`
`sudo chown -R dd-agent:dd-agent /var/log/datadog/`
questions.explanation: `chown` changes the owner and group of files, `-R` applies the change recursively, and `dd-agent:dd-agent` sets both the user and group to the Agent's account. `chmod` changes permission bits and does not accept a user:group pair, `chgrp` changes only the group, and `su` switches users rather than changing file ownership.

questions.question: You configured the Agent to tail `/var/log/apache/access.log`, but no logs arrive in Datadog. What is a common Linux-specific cause?
choices: The Agent runs as `dd-agent`, which lacks read access to root-only logs
The Agent is only allowed to tail files located under `/opt/datadog-agent`
The Agent runs as root, and root is blocked from reading app logs
Files in `/var/log` are binary and must be converted before tailing
questions.explanation: The Agent runs under the `dd-agent` user and group, not root, so it cannot read log files in `/var/log` that only root can access. Datadog suggests granting access, for example with `setfacl -m u:dd-agent:rx`, and making it persist across log rotation. The Agent can tail files anywhere it has read permission, and it does not run as root by default.

questions.question: Datadog docs run a check with `sudo -u dd-agent -- datadog-agent check <CHECK_NAME>`. What is the purpose of `-u dd-agent`?
choices: It updates the check to its latest version before running it
It uploads the check output using the dd-agent API key
It runs the check as the `dd-agent` user, like the Agent service
It unlocks the dd-agent account so the check can use root
questions.explanation: `sudo -u user` runs the command as the specified user instead of the default target user, root. Running the check as `dd-agent` reproduces the permissions the Agent service actually has, so file or socket access problems show up during testing instead of being hidden by root privileges. The flag has nothing to do with updates, API keys, or unlocking accounts.

questions.question: After editing `/etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml` on a systemd-based Ubuntu host, which command applies the change?
choices: `sudo systemctl enable datadog-agent`
`sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent`
`sudo systemctl daemon-reload`
`sudo journalctl -u datadog-agent`
questions.explanation: Configuration changes take effect when the Agent restarts, and `systemctl restart` stops and then starts the unit. `enable` only configures the service to start at boot, `daemon-reload` reloads systemd unit files rather than application config, and `journalctl -u` just shows the service's log entries.

questions.question: On a systemd-based host, which command displays the journal log entries for the Datadog Agent service unit?
choices: `systemctl enable datadog-agent`
`ps -u datadog-agent`
`tail -f /etc/datadog-agent`
`journalctl -u datadog-agent`
questions.explanation: `journalctl` prints log entries stored by systemd-journald, and `-u` filters them to a specific unit such as the `datadog-agent` service; add `-f` to follow new entries. `systemctl enable` configures boot-time start, `ps -u` lists processes owned by a user, and `/etc/datadog-agent` is a configuration directory, not a log file.

questions.question: On an older Upstart-based system such as CentOS/RHEL 6 or SUSE 11, which command do Datadog docs give for starting the Agent service?
choices: `sudo start datadog-agent`
`sudo systemctl start datadog-agent`
`sudo systemd start datadog-agent`
`sudo launchctl start datadog-agent`
questions.explanation: Datadog's Linux docs say that on Upstart-based systems such as CentOS/RHEL 6 or SUSE 11 you swap `systemctl <action>` with `<action>`, so starting the Agent is `sudo start datadog-agent`. `systemctl` is the systemd tool used on modern distributions, `systemd` is not a service-control command, and `launchctl` is the macOS equivalent.

questions.question: Which pairing of a Linux distribution and its native package manager is correct?
choices: Ubuntu - `yum`
Red Hat Enterprise Linux - `apt-get`
SUSE Linux Enterprise - `zypper`
Debian - `dnf`
questions.explanation: SUSE and openSUSE use `zypper`, which is why Datadog removes the Agent there with `sudo zypper remove datadog-agent`. Debian and Ubuntu use `apt`/`apt-get`, while Red Hat-family distributions (RHEL, CentOS, Rocky, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, Amazon Linux) use `yum` or its successor `dnf`.

questions.question: In a Bash shell, which command sets `DD_SITE` so that programs started from that shell, such as an install script, can read it?
choices: `set DD_SITE=datadoghq.eu`
`echo DD_SITE=datadoghq.eu`
`printenv DD_SITE datadoghq.eu`
`export DD_SITE=datadoghq.eu`
questions.explanation: `export` marks a variable to be passed to child processes in their environment; environment variables are how the Datadog install script receives values such as `DD_API_KEY` and `DD_SITE`. `set VAR=value` is Windows cmd syntax (in Bash, `set` changes shell options and positional parameters), `echo` only prints text, and `printenv` displays variables without setting them.

questions.question: You want to confirm that DogStatsD is listening on UDP port 8125 on a Linux host. Which command lists listening UDP sockets with numeric ports and their owning processes?
choices: `sudo ss -ulnp`
`sudo ss -tlnp`
`ping -c 1 localhost`
`curl -I localhost:8125`
questions.explanation: `ss` dumps socket statistics, similar to the older `netstat`: `-u` selects UDP, `-l` shows listening sockets, `-n` keeps ports numeric, and `-p` shows the owning process. `-t` would show TCP sockets instead, `ping` tests ICMP reachability rather than ports, and `curl -I` sends an HTTP HEAD request, which does not apply to a UDP listener.

questions.question: Datadog's Linux install one-liner downloads its script with `curl -L`. What does the `-L` option do?
choices: Limits the download speed to avoid saturating the link
Lists only the HTTP response headers, without the body
Follows redirects when the server reports a new location
Logs the full request to a local file for later debugging
questions.explanation: With `-L` (`--location`), if the server answers with a 3XX status and a Location header, curl repeats the request at the new location instead of stopping at the redirect response. Fetching only the headers is `-I`, and verbose debugging output is `-v`; `-L` has nothing to do with speed limits or log files.

questions.question: Which command searches `/etc/datadog-agent` and all of its subdirectories for files named `conf.yaml`?
choices: `grep -r conf.yaml /etc/datadog-agent`
`find /etc/datadog-agent -name conf.yaml`
`ls /etc/datadog-agent/conf.yaml`
`cat /etc/datadog-agent/*/conf.yaml`
questions.explanation: `find` walks a directory tree recursively, and `-name conf.yaml` matches files by name, so it finds every `conf.d/<integration>.d/conf.yaml`. `grep -r` searches file contents for the text rather than matching file names, `ls` checks one exact path, and the `cat` glob reaches only one directory level and prints file contents.

flashcards.back:
`system.cpu.user`: percent of time the CPU spent running user space processes (application code).
`system.cpu.system`: percent of time the CPU spent running the kernel (system calls, drivers).
The percent of time the CPU spent waiting for I/O operations to complete. High iowait with low user/system time points to a storage bottleneck. Not available on Windows.
Percent of time a virtual CPU waited while the hypervisor serviced another virtual CPU. Only applies to VMs (not available on Windows). High steal = noisy neighbor or oversubscribed physical host.

flashcards.front: CPU state fields in the `top` summary line
flashcards.back:
us = un-niced user processes
sy = kernel
ni = niced user processes
id = idle
wa = waiting for I/O
hi / si = hardware / software interrupts
st = time stolen from this VM by the hypervisor

Number of tasks running/runnable (state R) or waiting for disk I/O (state D), averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Same numbers as `uptime` and `/proc/loadavg`. Datadog: `system.load.1`, `system.load.5`, `system.load.15` (Linux only).
Load average normalized by the number of CPUs (Linux only). Around 1 means the CPUs are fully subscribed; above 1 means tasks are queuing. Lets one threshold fit hosts of different sizes.

`usable`: MemAvailable from /proc/meminfo (or free + buffered + cached if absent) - memory applications can still get.
`free`: completely unused RAM only; often low on healthy Linux hosts because spare RAM is used as cache.
`pct_usable`: usable as a fraction of total.

Disk space (a swap partition or swap file) where the kernel moves inactive memory pages when RAM is full. Much slower than RAM, so sustained swapping hurts performance. Datadog: `system.swap.used`, `system.swap.free`, `system.swap.pct_free`.

HDD: spinning magnetic platters and a moving read/write head; cheaper per GB; best at large sequential I/O.
SSD: nonvolatile flash memory, no moving parts; faster and more durable; handles random I/O efficiently.

IOPS: input/output operations per second - the limit for many small or random I/Os (databases).
Throughput: data per second, e.g. MiB/s - the limit for large sequential transfers.
Throughput = IOPS x I/O size. Datadog: `system.io.r_s` / `system.io.w_s` are read/write requests per second.

The structure holding a file's metadata (type, mode/permissions, owner, timestamps, size) - but not its name, which lives in the directory. Every file uses one; running out blocks new files even when blocks are free. Check with `df -i` or `system.fs.inodes.in_use`.

Both describe disk space in use relative to the total.
`in_use`: a fraction from 0 to 1 (alert at > 0.9).
`utilized`: a percentage from 0 to 100.
Byte values: `system.disk.used`, `system.disk.free`, `system.disk.total`.

A core is an independent processing unit. With simultaneous multithreading (e.g. Hyper-Threading), each core runs multiple threads, and each thread appears to the OS as a vCPU. Example: m5.xlarge = 2 cores x 2 threads = 4 vCPUs.

flashcards.front: Bare metal vs virtual machine vs container
flashcards.back:
Bare metal: the OS runs directly on a physical server.
VM: a full OS with its own kernel and drivers, running on a hypervisor.
Container: an isolated process plus its files, sharing the host kernel; lighter and faster to start.

Type 1 (bare-metal): installed directly on the hardware, e.g. KVM, Microsoft Hyper-V, VMware ESXi.
Type 2 (hosted): runs as an application on a host OS, e.g. Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation.

Any physical or virtual OS instance you monitor: a server, VM, Kubernetes node, Azure App Service Plan instance, or Heroku dyno. If you install the Agent inside each container, each container counts as a host for billing.

`system.net.bytes_rcvd` / `system.net.bytes_sent`: bytes received/sent on a device per second.
`system.net.packets_in.error`: receive errors.
`system.net.tcp.retrans_segs`: retransmitted TCP segments.
The Network check is enabled by default.

flashcards.front: Datadog Agent file locations on Linux
flashcards.back:
Main config: /etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml
Integration configs: /etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/
Install directory: /opt/datadog-agent/
Logs: /var/log/datadog/ (agent.log, process-agent.log, trace-agent.log, ...)

/etc: machine-local configuration files
/var/log: log files
/opt: add-on software packages
/tmp: temporary files that may be deleted without notice (e.g. at boot)
/home: user home directories (root's is /root)

The mount point of the proc pseudo-filesystem, which exposes information about running processes and the kernel; its files are generated by the kernel, not stored on disk. Examples: /proc/meminfo, /proc/loadavg, /proc/<PID>/.

The Linux Agent runs as the unprivileged `dd-agent` user and `dd-agent` group, not root. It needs read access to logs it tails, and must own /var/log/datadog/ and /opt/datadog-agent/run. Uninstalling the Agent does not remove the user (`sudo userdel dd-agent`).

flashcards.front: How do you find a Linux host's distribution and version?
flashcards.back:
`cat /etc/os-release` (or `cat /etc/os*`): NAME, VERSION, ID, PRETTY_NAME.
`lsb_release -a`: distributor ID, description, release, codename.
Not `uname -n` or `hostname` (host name) or `uname -r` (kernel release).

read = 4, write = 2, execute = 1; add them per digit. Digits are owner, group, others.
755 = rwxr-xr-x (scripts, directories)
644 = rw-r--r-- (config files)
600 = rw------- (private files)

1st character: file type (- file, d directory, l symlink).
Next 9: owner, group, other permissions (rw- / r-- / ---).
Then: link count, owner (dd-agent), group (dd-agent), size, modification time, name.

`sudo <cmd>`: run one command as another user (root by default); `sudo -u dd-agent <cmd>` runs it as dd-agent.
`su`: start a shell as another user (root if none given); `su -` gives a login environment.

`tail file`: last 10 lines; `tail -n 50 file`: last 50.
`tail -f file`: keep printing new lines as the file grows (Ctrl+C to stop).
`head -n 20 file`: first 20 lines.
`less file`: page through a file interactively.

-i ignore case
-v invert match (non-matching lines)
-r recursive through directories
-c count matching lines
-n show line numbers
-l list names of matching files

`df -h`: used/available space per mounted filesystem (`df -i` for inodes, `df -T` for filesystem type).
`du -sh <dir>`: total space used by a directory tree.
`free -h`: RAM and swap usage, read from /proc/meminfo.

15 SIGTERM: default for `kill`; asks the process to exit cleanly.
9 SIGKILL: `kill -9`; cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored.
1 SIGHUP: hangup; many daemons reload config on it.
2 SIGINT: interrupt from the keyboard (Ctrl+C).

flashcards.front: Managing the Agent service on Linux
flashcards.back:
`sudo systemctl start|stop|restart|status datadog-agent`
`enable` = start at boot; `disable` = don't.
Upstart (CentOS/RHEL 6, SUSE 11): `sudo start datadog-agent`.
Service logs: `journalctl -u datadog-agent` (add -f to follow).

flashcards.front: Linux package managers by distribution family
flashcards.back:
Debian / Ubuntu: apt, apt-get (.deb packages)
RHEL / CentOS / Rocky / AlmaLinux / Oracle Linux / Amazon Linux / Fedora: yum or dnf (.rpm packages)
SUSE / openSUSE: zypper (.rpm packages)

cmd1 | cmd2: stdout of cmd1 becomes stdin of cmd2.
> file: write stdout to a file, truncating it.
>> file: append stdout to a file.
2>&1: send stderr (fd 2) wherever stdout (fd 1) goes.

flashcards.front: Environment variables in Bash (and DD_* for the Agent)
flashcards.back:
`export NAME=value`: set a variable and pass it to child processes.
`echo $NAME` / `printenv NAME`: read it; `env`: list all.
Most datadog.yaml options can be set as DD_* variables (e.g. DD_API_KEY); they take precedence over the file.

`ping -c 4 <host>`: send 4 ICMP echo requests, then stop.
`curl -v https://<url>`: test HTTP(S) and show request/response headers (`-L` follows redirects).
`ss -tulnp` (or older `netstat`): listening TCP/UDP sockets with owning processes.

Linux: a free, open source OS released under the GNU GPL, shipped as many distributions (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL, SUSE, Amazon Linux, ...).
Windows: a proprietary Microsoft OS.
The key difference is open source vs proprietary.
